answer:
**Squared distance gives extreme points disproportionate influence.** For one-dimensional data (0,0,0,100) and one cluster, the k-means centroid is 25. The three ordinary points are now far from their center because the single outlier pulled the mean. A median-based center is 0, which better represents the majority under absolute distance. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html)

K-medians minimizes Manhattan distance and updates coordinates with medians. K-medoids restricts each center to an actual observed point and can use suitable dissimilarities. Both can reduce some outlier sensitivity, but neither makes arbitrary contamination harmless, and medoid search can be more expensive.

**Initialization is a separate issue.** With several clusters, alternating assignment and centroid updates decreases the k-means objective but can settle at a local optimum. Different starting centers may divide the same data differently. K-means++ initialization and multiple restarts help explore better solutions.

Scale features deliberately, inspect cluster stability, and decide what an unusual point means. A rare but legitimate population may deserve a cluster; a sensor error may not. Removing every extreme point merely because it worsens the objective can erase the phenomena you intended to discover. Choose distance and robustness according to the data-generating task.

**Technical details and references.**

K-means uses squared distances, so a far outlier has disproportionately large influence and can pull a centroid or consume a cluster. Its alternating assignment/update procedure can converge to a local optimum depending on initialization. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html)

K-medoids restricts centers to observed points and can use more robust dissimilarities; k-medians minimizes Manhattan distances and updates coordinates to medians. These reduce some outlier influence but do not make arbitrary contamination harmless. Medoid optimization can be more expensive.

Use k-means++ or multiple starts, scale features sensibly, inspect extreme points, and compare objective/stability across seeds. Decide whether anomalies should form a meaningful cluster or be excluded using a justified data-quality policy rather than deleting them solely to improve a clustering score.
